cases.n: IICSA — Anglican Church investigation report
cases.place: England and Wales (Church of England, Church in Wales)
cases.who: Church of England; Church in Wales
cases.cover: Inquiry found the Church gave 'excessive attention' to alleged perpetrators over victims, ignored safeguarding advice, and used forgiveness to justify failing to respond to allegations.
cases.d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its Anglican Church investigation report on 6 October 2020. It counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and warned the true scale cannot be known. In 2018 alone, dioceses received 2,504 safeguarding concerns, 449 of them about recent child sexual abuse. It found deference to authority, clericalism and taboos about sexuality kept victims from disclosing, and that bishops kept safeguarding decision-making power.
cases.cite: IICSA, The Anglican Church: Safeguarding in the Church of England and the Church in Wales, 6 October 2020; Church Times, 9 October 2020

cases.n: Diocese of Chichester — clergy abuse (IICSA case study)
cases.who: Church of England, Diocese of Chichester
cases.cover: Clergy with known concerns (Rideout, Cotton, Graves, House) were given or kept permission to officiate; Cotton's prior conviction for indecent exposure involving a child sat in his diocesan file but was not shared with police; an archdeacon declined to report a serious indecent assault; Sussex Police dropped a 1997–98 investigation and later destroyed its records.
cases.d: IICSA found the Diocese of Chichester had more child sexual abuse convictions than any other Church of England diocese. Roy Cotton had been ordained in the 1960s despite a prior conviction involving a child. Sussex Police investigated Cotton and Colin Pritchard in 1997–98 without charges; when Northamptonshire Police revived the case in 2006, Sussex Police had destroyed its records. The diocese's 2008–09 Past Cases Review missed the scale of abuse, and real action against abusers began only with Operation Perry in 2011.
cases.cite: IICSA, Anglican Church Case Studies: Chichester/Peter Ball, conclusions

cases.n: Bishop Peter Ball — conviction and Church collusion
cases.victims_note: 18 young men at sentencing (2015); IICSA describes 17 teenagers and young men, 1977–1992
cases.who: Church of England; 'Give a Year to God' scheme
cases.cover: Lambeth Palace received seven letters supporting complainant Neil Todd's allegations in 1992 but passed only the least incriminating one to police; Archbishop George Carey wrote to the Gloucestershire Chief Constable; Ball's twin brother, also a bishop, phoned potential complainants to dissuade them; Ball accepted a caution in 1992 and was soon returned to ministry, including work in schools.
cases.d: Peter Ball, former Bishop of Lewes and of Gloucester, ran a 'Give a Year to God' scheme for young men that the Church did not monitor. Gloucestershire police investigated in 1992 and he accepted a caution for one offence; IICSA found the Crown Prosecution Service advice to caution was wrong and other charges were possible. He pleaded guilty in 2015 and on 7 October 2015 was jailed for 32 months for offences against 18 young men over 15 years. Dame Moira Gibb's review 'An Abuse of Faith' (June 2017) found the Church colluded with Ball; Lord Carey stepped back from ministry. IICSA also noted the Duchy of Cornwall bought a property rented to Ball and his brother.
cases.cite: IICSA Chichester/Peter Ball conclusions; Gibb, An Abuse of Faith (GS Misc 1172), June 2017; sentencing coverage 7 October 2015

cases.n: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.place: Iwerne camps (Dorset) and Winchester College; later Zambesi Ministries camps, Zimbabwe; Cape Town
cases.victims_note: Makin Review: between 115 and 130 boys and young men; at least 85 of them in Zimbabwe and South Africa (Church Times, citing the review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.cover: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
cases.d: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cite: Makin, Independent Learning Lessons Review: John Smyth QC (Church of England), published 7 November 2024; Church Times, 15 November 2024

cases.n: Royal Commission data — Anglican Church of Australia
cases.victims_note: 1,082 complainants about 1,115 alleged incidents reported 1980–2015; some incidents dated back to 1950
cases.who: Anglican Church of Australia
cases.d: Data released at the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in March 2017 showed 1,082 people lodged complaints of child sexual abuse about 1,115 incidents in the Anglican Church of Australia between 1980 and 2015. The complaints identified 569 alleged perpetrators who were clergy, teachers or volunteers, plus 133 whose church roles were unknown (702 in total).
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 52 data, March 2017; Gulf News/AP

cases.n: Canada residential schools run by Anglican, United and Presbyterian churches
cases.victims_note: About 37,000 of roughly 80,000 Common Experience Payment applicants also claimed sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts (all churches combined); about 180,000 First Nations, Inuit and Métis children attended over 150 years
cases.who: Anglican Church of Canada (ran over 30 schools), United Church, Presbyterian Church, with the Catholic Church and federal government
cases.cover: The schools were a federal government system run by churches.
cases.d: Canada's Indian residential schools were run for the federal government by the Anglican, Catholic, Presbyterian and United churches; the Anglican Church of Canada operated more than 30. In April 2013 Truth and Reconciliation Commission chair Justice Murray Sinclair said about 37,000 former students had filed claims for sexual abuse, serious physical abuse or other wrongful acts, and asked the public to imagine 'a school where half of the students suffered sexual and physical abuse'. The TRC's final report followed in 2015. Under the 2006 Indian Residential Schools Settlement Agreement, to which the Anglican, Presbyterian and United churches were parties (Anglicans ran about 30% of schools, the United Church about 10%), the Independent Assessment Process for sexual and serious physical abuse had paid C$3.18 billion to 31,103 former students by 31 March 2019 (all churches combined).
cases.cite: Anglican Journal, 25 April 2013 (TRC Quebec National Event)

cases.n: Southern Baptist Convention — 'Abuse of Faith' investigation
cases.place: Southern Baptist churches nationwide (most convicted offenders in Texas)
cases.victims_note: 'more than 700' victims over about 20 years
cases.who: Southern Baptist Convention churches
cases.d: The Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News published 'Abuse of Faith' on 10–11 February 2019. They found about 380 Southern Baptist ministers and volunteers had faced allegations of sexual misconduct over the previous 20 years, with more than 700 victims. Many pleaded guilty or were convicted, more from Texas than any other state.
cases.cite: Houston Chronicle / San Antonio Express-News, 'Abuse of Faith', February 2019; Baptist Standard, 11 February 2019

cases.n: Southern Baptist Convention — Guidepost report and secret list of accused ministers
cases.victims_note: The list released on 26 May 2022 had 703 entries of accused ministers, mostly 2000–2019
cases.who: Southern Baptist Convention Executive Committee
cases.cover: Former Executive Committee officials D. August Boto and Roger Oldham kept a private list of abusive ministers, but no one acted to keep them out of SBC pulpits; survivors met 'resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility' and were told church autonomy prevented action; a few senior leaders and outside counsel focused on avoiding liability.
cases.d: Guidepost Solutions, hired after SBC delegates demanded an outside probe in 2021, released its report on 22 May 2022. It found a few senior Executive Committee leaders had for about two decades controlled the response to abuse reports to limit legal liability, ignoring or disbelieving survivors. The Executive Committee then published the previously secret list, 205 pages and 703 entries, on 26 May 2022.
cases.cite: Guidepost Solutions report, 22 May 2022; AP (Spokesman-Review), 23 May 2022; WSOC-TV/AP, 27 May 2022

cases.n: Frank Houston — Royal Commission Case Study 18 (Assemblies of God / Hillsong)
cases.who: Assemblies of God in Australia (now Australian Christian Churches); Hillsong Church
cases.cover: When allegations surfaced in 1999, Brian Houston, then National President of the Assemblies of God and Frank Houston's son, confronted his father, who confessed; Brian Houston and the National Executive did not refer the matter to police.
cases.d: Pastor Frank Houston sexually abused a young boy in the 1970s. The Royal Commission's Case Study 18 findings (November 2015) found that Brian Houston and the national executive did not report the allegations to police when they emerged in 1999, and that Brian Houston had a conflict of interest as both national president and the son of the alleged perpetrator. Frank Houston died in 2004 without being charged.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 18 findings, November 2015

cases.n: Brian Houston acquitted of concealing father's abuse
cases.who: Hillsong Church
cases.d: Hillsong founder Brian Houston was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence of another person, namely his father Frank Houston's abuse of a boy in the 1970s, which court papers said he knew of by 1999. On 17 August 2023 Magistrate Gareth Christofi found him not guilty, ruling he had a reasonable excuse for not reporting.
cases.cite: Religion News Service, 16–17 August 2023

cases.n: ForuM study — German Protestant Church (EKD)
cases.place: EKD, Hanover (all regional churches and Diakonie)
cases.victims_note: 2,225 documented victims in files reviewed; researchers estimated up to 9,355 minors
cases.who: Evangelische Kirche in Deutschland (EKD) and Diakonie
cases.cover: Researchers said regional churches delivered documents slowly despite a contract, so the study could not be completed; co-author Martin Wazlawik called the figures 'the tip of the tip of the iceberg'.
cases.d: The ForuM study, commissioned by the EKD in 2020 and led by Hanover University of Applied Sciences and Arts, was released on 25 January 2024. Files reviewed showed 2,225 victims and 1,259 potential perpetrators among ministers, employees and volunteers since 1946, with a projected estimate of up to 9,355 abused minors. EKD head Kirsten Fehrs called it a 'massive failure' toward victims.
cases.cite: ForuM research network, 25 January 2024; AFP (Citizen Digital), 25 January 2024

cases.n: Jehovah's Witnesses — Royal Commission Case Study 29
cases.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Australia (Jehovah's Witnesses)
cases.cover: None of the 1,006 alleged perpetrators recorded since 1950 was reported to police by the church. The 'two-witness rule' required two witnesses before elders' judicial committees could act, blocking 125 allegations; 401 members were expelled after internal hearings and 230 later readmitted.
cases.d: At hearings in July–August 2015, the Royal Commission was told the Watch Tower Society's files held 1,006 alleged perpetrators of child sexual abuse since 1950, including 579 confessions, and that none had been reported to secular authorities. The Commission referred 514 alleged perpetrators to police. Its November 2016 report found the organisation did not respond adequately to child sexual abuse and that its two-witness rule showed a serious lack of understanding of abuse.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Case Study 29 report, November 2016; AFP (News24), 27 July 2015

cases.n: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
cases.who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
cases.d: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.
cases.cite: Doe (Conti) v. Watchtower, California Court of Appeal, April 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

cases.n: Warren Jeffs — FLDS child 'marriages' conviction
cases.place: Yearning For Zion ranch, Eldorado, Texas; Short Creek (Colorado City AZ / Hildale UT)
cases.victims_note: Texas conviction concerned girls aged 12 and 15
cases.who: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
cases.d: FLDS president Warren Jeffs was added to the FBI Ten Most Wanted list on 6 May 2006 and arrested in Nevada on 28 August 2006. A 2007 Utah conviction for accomplice to rape was reversed in 2010, and Arizona charges were dismissed in 2010. In August 2011 a Texas jury convicted him of two counts of sexual assault of a child, girls aged 12 and 15 he had taken as 'spiritual wives', and he was sentenced to life plus 20 years. Texas authorities had raided the YFZ ranch on 7 April 2008 and taken custody of about 416 children, who were later returned after courts found the removal unjustified.
cases.cite: AP, 4–9 August 2011; Wikipedia 'Warren Jeffs' (index)

cases.n: Bountiful, B.C. — parents convicted of taking 13-year-old to marry Warren Jeffs
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.d: In February 2017 a B.C. Supreme Court judge in Cranbrook convicted Brandon James Blackmore and Emily Gail Blackmore of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes: in 2004 they took their 13-year-old daughter to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were jailed in August 2017. In the same trial James Oler was acquitted of a related charge.
cases.cite: Salt Lake Tribune, 7 February 2017; AP, 11 August 2017

cases.n: James Oler — removing a 15-year-old from Canada to marry
cases.who: FLDS, Bountiful community
cases.d: Former FLDS Bountiful bishop James Oler was first acquitted in 2017; the B.C. Court of Appeal ordered a new trial. In May 2019 he was found guilty of removing a child from Canada, having taken a 15-year-old girl to the United States in 2004 to be married to an older FLDS member. On 29 August 2019 he was sentenced to 12 months in jail and 18 months' probation. Separately, Oler (5 wives) and Winston Blackmore (24 wives, 1990–2014) were convicted of polygamy in July 2017.
cases.cite: CBC News, 29 August 2019; RNZ/AFP, 25 July 2017

cases.n: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
cases.victims_note: Warrant listed at least eight pupils; convicted over abuse of two sisters
cases.who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cases.cover: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.
cases.d: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.
cases.cite: County Court of Victoria verdict 3 April 2023 (Al Jazeera); Wikipedia 'Malka Leifer affair' (index)

cases.n: Yaakov Litzman — breach of trust for shielding Malka Leifer
cases.who: Israeli Ministry of Health; ultra-Orthodox Agudat Yisrael party
cases.cover: A government minister pressured ministry psychiatrists to alter evaluations of an extradition suspect.
cases.d: Former Israeli health minister Yaakov Litzman signed a plea deal in January 2022 admitting breach of trust for pressuring Health Ministry employees to change psychiatric evaluations so that Malka Leifer would appear unfit to stand extradition trial. He resigned from the Knesset in June 2022 and on 8 August 2022 the Jerusalem Magistrate's Court sentenced him to eight months' probation and a fine of about US$900. Australian Jewish groups condemned the deal as lenient.
cases.cite: AP, 8 August 2022

cases.n: Charity Commission inquiry — Manchester New Moston Jehovah's Witnesses congregation
cases.who: Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses (charity); Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
cases.cover: Trustees dismissed one allegation as a matter between two teenagers, did not enforce restrictions on the accused, and the victims were effectively required to repeat their allegations at an internal hearing in front of the abuser, who was allowed to question them. The charity did not give the Commission accurate and complete answers. The Watch Tower Society fought the inquiry through five courts and tribunals until 2016.
cases.d: Allegations of child abuse against a trustee of the New Moston congregation were made in 2012 and 2013; he was later convicted of two counts of indecent assault. The Charity Commission opened a statutory inquiry on 27 May 2014 and published its report on 26 July 2017, finding the trustees had not adequately dealt with the allegations. The Commission also ran a wider inquiry into the Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain.
cases.cite: Charity Commission for England and Wales, Manchester New Moston Congregation of Jehovah's Witnesses inquiry report, 26 July 2017

cases.n: A v Watchtower — High Court damages over Peter Stewart abuse
cases.who: Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society of Britain
cases.d: On 19 June 2015 the High Court awarded £275,000 damages to a woman abused as a child by Jehovah's Witness ministerial servant Peter Stewart, holding the organisation liable; appeals were refused. In a separate 2014 case in Barry, Wales, elder Mark Sewell was sentenced to 14 years for eight sex offences, and most of the investigating elders declined to give evidence.
cases.cite: A v Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society, High Court, 19 June 2015 (summarised in Wikipedia with citations)

cases.n: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
cases.victims_note: 751 people shared experiences through the study's contact point; 27% of cases led to a police report
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
cases.d: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.
cases.cite: Utrecht University / WODC, 'Sexual abuse and willingness to report sexual abuse within the Jehovah's Witnesses community', 23 January 2020

cases.n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Jehovah's Witnesses child sexual abuse charges
cases.place: Harrisburg, Pennsylvania (defendants from Philadelphia, Delaware, Butler and Berks counties)
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses congregations in Pennsylvania
cases.d: A statewide investigating grand jury in Harrisburg, opened after a county prosecutor's referral, heard dozens of witnesses about abuse in Jehovah's Witness congregations. On 7 July 2023 Attorney General Michelle Henry announced charges against five more men, bringing the total to 14 charged; one earlier suspect killed himself before arrest. One former elder was later convicted in Lancaster County.
cases.cite: AP (WITF), 7 July 2023

cases.n: Latter-day Saints abuse help line — Bisbee, Arizona case (AP investigation)
cases.who: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
cases.cover: After the father confessed to his bishop, the bishop called the church's abuse help line; church lawyers told him the clergy-penitent privilege meant he had to keep it secret. AP reported the abuse continued for about seven years afterwards. The help line, set up in 1995, routes calls that pose legal risk to church attorneys.
cases.d: Paul Douglas Adams, a Border Patrol employee and church member in Bisbee, abused his daughter from age 5 and later a second daughter, and filmed the abuse; he stopped only when arrested in 2017 and died by suicide in jail before trial. An AP investigation published 4 August 2022 found church officials had known for years through confessions. Arizona law, like more than 20 states, lets clergy withhold abuse learned in confession. The church disputed the AP's account.
cases.cite: Associated Press investigation, 4 August 2022

cases.n: Colonia Dignidad — Paul Schäfer convicted of abusing 25 children
cases.place: Colonia Dignidad (now Villa Baviera), near Parral, Maule Region
cases.victims_note: Conviction covered 25 minors abused 1993–1997; 26 children's reports led to the 1996 warrant; the colony held about 100 children at its peak
cases.who: Colonia Dignidad / Sociedad Benefactora y Educacional Dignidad (German sect)
cases.cover: Chile's Rettig Report (1991) found the colony served as a detention and torture centre for Pinochet's secret police (DINA) from 1973; German diplomats 'at best looked away' from the 1960s to the 1980s (German Foreign Minister Steinmeier, 2016). Schäfer fled in 1997 and hid in Argentina for eight years.
cases.d: Former Luftwaffe medic and lay preacher Paul Schäfer, wanted in Germany since 1959 for abusing two boys in Siegburg, founded Colonia Dignidad in Chile in 1961. The colony ran a free school and clinic for local children, some of whom were illegally adopted into the sect. Charged in 1996 with abusing children, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997; he was convicted in absentia in 2004 with 26 other members, found in Tortuguitas near Buenos Aires in March 2005, and on 24 May 2006 sentenced to 20 years for 20 counts of indecent assault and 5 of forced sodomy against 25 minors, plus about US$1.4 million to families. He died in prison in 2010. In January 2013 six former leaders were jailed.
cases.cite: Houston Chronicle/AP, 24 May 2006; MercoPress, 11 March 2005; Wikipedia 'Paul Schäfer' and 'Colonia Dignidad' (index)

cases.n: Germany acknowledges failures over Colonia Dignidad
cases.who: German Foreign Office; Colonia Dignidad
cases.cover: Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier said in April 2016 that 'over the course of many years, from the 60s to the 80s, German diplomats at best looked away' and that the embassy failed to shield Germans at the colony.
cases.d: In April 2016 Germany released Foreign Office files from 1986–1996 and the foreign minister admitted diplomats had failed colony residents, including abused children. In 2017 the Bundestag formally acknowledged German responsibility and asked the government to plan an investigation, memorial and help for victims; in 2019 Germany announced compensation payments to victims.
cases.cite: NBC News/Reuters, April 2016; German Foreign Office, 26 April 2016; Deutsche Welle 2018 and BBC 18 May 2019 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
cases.who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
cases.d: In a custody case decided on 19 October 1995 after three years of hearings, Lord Justice Alan Ward found that the group, including some top leaders, had in the past sexually abused minors and used severe corporal punishment and sequestration of children. He found these practices had been abandoned by 1995, let the mother keep custody, and required the group to end corporal punishment in the UK and to denounce founder David Berg's writings that had led to children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour. A 2005 group spokesperson acknowledged 'sexually inappropriate advances' in a 1978–1986 transitional period.
cases.cite: Re ST (A Minor), judgment of Lord Justice Ward, 19 October 1995 (summarised by CESNUR, International Journal of Cultic Studies, and Wikipedia)

cases.n: Argentina raids on The Family (Children of God) communes
cases.victims_note: 137 children taken into custody; the judge said 9 showed signs of maltreatment
cases.who: The Family / Children of God
cases.d: On 1 September 1993 Judge Roberto Marquevich ordered raids on Family communes near Buenos Aires; 137 children were taken into state custody and about 30 members arrested. The judge said nine children showed signs of 'cruel and atrocious maltreatment', which the group disputed. Children were later released after examination and no convictions resulted. Raids in Australia (1992, including Panton Hill, Victoria), France and Spain also ended without convictions.
cases.cite: Christianity Today, 25 October 1993; Washington Post/Reuters, 2 September 1993 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Twelve Tribes — Bavaria child removals upheld by European Court
cases.place: Klosterzimmern (Deiningen) and a second community, Bavaria
cases.victims_note: 40 children removed
cases.who: Twelve Tribes (Zwölf Stämme)
cases.d: On 5 September 2013 more than 100 Bavarian police removed 40 children from two Twelve Tribes communities after undercover recordings by journalist Wolfram Kuhnigk showed children being beaten with rods; the group says it canes disobedient children. This was physical, not sexual, abuse; the children were placed in foster care. In 2018 the European Court of Human Rights (Wetjen and Others v. Germany) upheld the removals because of the risk of inhuman or degrading treatment.
cases.cite: NPR, 5 September 2013; ECHR, Wetjen and Others v. Germany, 22 March 2018

cases.n: NXIVM — Keith Raniere convicted (including sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old)
cases.who: NXIVM (self-help group run as a cult)
cases.d: A Brooklyn federal jury convicted NXIVM leader Keith Raniere in June 2019 of racketeering, racketeering conspiracy, sex trafficking, attempted sex trafficking, forced labour conspiracy and wire fraud conspiracy. Prosecutors proved as racketeering acts that at 45 he sexually exploited a 15-year-old girl and photographed the abuse. On 27 October 2020 he was sentenced to 120 years and fined $1.75 million.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office EDNY press release, 27 October 2020

cases.n: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries — leader convicted of transporting girls across state lines
cases.victims_note: girls as young as 9
cases.who: Tony Alamo Christian Ministries
cases.d: On 24 July 2009 a federal jury convicted Tony Alamo on all 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; women testified he had taken them as 'wives' when they were children, some as young as 9. On 13 November 2009 he was sentenced to 175 years and fined $250,000. In 2013 federal authorities moved against 27 properties held by members to collect $2.5 million restitution. He died in custody in 2017.
cases.cite: FBI Little Rock press release, 13 November 2009

cases.n: Agape Boarding School — Christian boys' school, Missouri
cases.victims_note: 132 students enrolled in late 2021
cases.who: Agape Boarding School (independent Baptist ministry)
cases.cover: The state Attorney General's office said 22 workers should have been charged with serious crimes, but the county prosecutor charged five with low-level counts; in Missouri only the local prosecutor can file charges.
cases.d: Former students came forward in 2020. In 2021 the school's longtime doctor, David Smock, was charged with child sex crimes and five staff with low-level abuse counts; two later pleaded guilty to misdemeanours. Missouri passed a 2021 law tightening oversight of religious boarding schools. Agape closed on 20 January 2023.
cases.cite: AP (CBS News), 11 January 2023

cases.n: Royal Commission Case Study 22 — Yeshivah Melbourne and Yeshiva Bondi
cases.place: Yeshivah Centre, East St Kilda (Melbourne) and Yeshiva Centre, Bondi (Sydney)
cases.victims_note: Four survivors gave evidence
cases.who: Yeshivah Centre / Chabad Institutions of Victoria; Yeshiva Centre – Chabad NSW
cases.cover: The Commission found that the principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) as applied in the community discouraged reporting, and survivors who went to police were treated as outcasts. Bondi's Rabbi Yossi Feldman testified he 'was not aware it was illegal to touch a child's genitals'; the Commission found him ignorant of the duty to report.
cases.d: The Royal Commission held hearings in February 2015 on responses to abuse by David Cyprys, David Kramer and Aron Kestecher at Yeshivah Melbourne and Daniel Hayman at Yeshiva Bondi. Its report (released October–November 2016) found 'a marked absence of supportive leadership' for survivors at Yeshivah Melbourne. Its 2017 final report recommended Jewish institutions state that mesirah does not apply to reporting child sexual abuse.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 22, 2016

cases.n: Nechemya Weberman — Satmar counsellor, Williamsburg
cases.who: Satmar Hasidic community, Brooklyn
cases.cover: During the case men were arrested for trying to bribe the victim and her husband to drop it; four were later convicted of coercion or witness tampering. Others photographed her on the witness stand and posted the images online.
cases.d: Nechemya Weberman, an unlicensed counsellor in the Satmar community, abused a girl from age 12 to 15. He was convicted on all 59 counts on 10 December 2012 and sentenced on 22 January 2013 to 103 years, later cut on appeal. Brooklyn DA figures showed about 100 of 5,389 sex abuse cases since 2009 came from the Haredi community; critics said DA Charles Hynes's policy of not naming Haredi defendants protected the community.
cases.cite: AP (Times of Israel), 22 January 2013; Wikipedia 'Sexual abuse cases in Brooklyn's Haredi community' (index)

cases.n: AP investigation — sexual abuse in Pakistan's madrassas
cases.place: Pakistan (cases in Kehrore Pakka, Mansehra, Punjab)
cases.victims_note: 359 cases reported in newspapers over 10 years (Sahil tally); a Pakistani official disclosed more than 500 complaints against madrassa teachers in 2004
cases.who: Islamic seminaries (madrassas), over 22,000 registered with at least 2 million pupils
cases.cover: Police are often paid off and refuse to register cases; families of poor victims are pressured to 'forgive' clerics and accept money, which Pakistani law allows; the religious affairs minister dismissed the claims. Police told AP that clerics are almost never convicted.
cases.d: An AP investigation published 21 November 2017 found sexual abuse by clerics was pervasive in Pakistan's madrassas and seldom prosecuted. In one case a 9-year-old's teacher confessed but was freed after the mother 'forgave' him for $300. A follow-up AP investigation in 2020, based on dozens of police reports, found the same pattern.
cases.cite: Associated Press, 21 November 2017; AP/RFE-RL, 14 April 2020

cases.n: Herry Wirawan — Islamic boarding school, Bandung
cases.who: Islamic boarding schools (pesantren) run by the offender
cases.d: Herry Wirawan, head of Islamic boarding schools near Bandung, raped 13 girl students aged 12 to 16 between 2016 and 2021, making eight pregnant. A Bandung court gave him life in prison in February 2022; on prosecutors' appeal the Bandung High Court sentenced him to death on 4 April 2022.
cases.cite: Jakarta Post, 4 April 2022; AP, 5 April 2022

cases.n: Asaram Bapu — convicted of raping a 16-year-old at his ashram
cases.who: Asaram Bapu ashrams
cases.cover: Witnesses in his cases were attacked; a former aide was shot dead in May 2014 and the key witness in the Surat case was shot dead in January 2015.
cases.d: A 16-year-old girl said guru Asaram Bapu assaulted her on 15 August 2013 at his Manai ashram; he was arrested by Jodhpur police on 1 September 2013. On 25 April 2018 a Jodhpur court convicted him of raping a minor and sentenced him to life imprisonment. In January 2023 a Gandhinagar court gave him a second life term in a case brought by two sisters from Surat.
cases.cite: Jodhpur SC/ST court judgment, 25 April 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Asaram' with citations)

cases.n: Nithyananda — Gujarat abduction case and flight from India
cases.who: Nithyananda Dhyanapeetam
cases.d: On 17 November 2019 Gujarat Police registered a case of abduction after a Tamil Nadu couple said three of their children had been taken from Bangalore to Nithyananda's Ahmedabad ashram without consent. Police said on 20 November 2019 that Nithyananda had fled India after skipping hearings, and by January 2020 Interpol had issued a blue corner notice to locate him; he claims to have founded a 'Hindu nation', Kailasa. On 2 February 2024 the Gujarat High Court dismissed the father's habeas corpus petition, finding the daughters were adults who chose to stay with the group. He separately faces a 2010 rape case brought by an adult disciple.
cases.cite: The Hindu, 21 November 2019; NDTV, 22 January 2020; Indian Express, 3 February 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Nithyananda')

cases.n: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
cases.victims_note: 151 women and girls aged 3 to 65
cases.who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
cases.cover: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
cases.d: Between 2005 and 2009 men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sedated households with an animal anaesthetic spray and raped women and girls, the youngest three years old. In August 2011 a Bolivian court sentenced seven men to 25 years each; a veterinarian from a neighbouring colony who supplied the sedative got 12 years.
cases.cite: TIME, 26 August 2011; BBC News, 16 May 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Manitoba Colony, Bolivia')

cases.n: Royal Commission data — Uniting Church in Australia
cases.victims_note: about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse across the church's 40-year history
cases.who: Uniting Church in Australia
cases.d: At a Royal Commission hearing on 10 March 2017, the Uniting Church was reported to have faced about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse over its 40-year history (it was formed in 1977). The Commission's Case Study 23 also examined Knox Grammar School, a Uniting Church school in Sydney.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, hearing 10 March 2017 (Guardian Australia via BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Knox Grammar School — Royal Commission Case Study 23
cases.who: Knox Grammar School (Uniting Church)
cases.cover: The Commission found headmaster Ian Paterson 'deliberately covered up' allegations to protect the school's reputation, never reported a student's abuse allegation to police in 30 years even after reporting became mandatory in 1988, let accused teachers resign and gave some positive references.
cases.d: In 2009 five former Knox teachers were charged with sex offences committed between 1976 and 1990, and all were convicted. Royal Commission hearings in February–March 2015 examined the school's and the Uniting Church's responses from 1970 to 2012; findings reported in September 2016 said the headmaster had deliberately withheld information from police.
cases.cite: Royal Commission Case Study 23 (2015–2016); Sydney Morning Herald, 14 September 2016 (via Wikipedia 'Knox Grammar School')

cases.n: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane — Archbishop Peter Hollingworth's handling of abuse
cases.who: Anglican Diocese of Brisbane; Toowoomba Preparatory School; Church of England Boys' Society
cases.cover: A diocesan inquiry found that in 1993 Archbishop Hollingworth allowed a known paedophile to keep working as a priest. He later became Governor-General of Australia.
cases.d: In 2001 the Diocese of Brisbane was ordered to pay A$834,800 to a victim of a teacher at Toowoomba Preparatory School, and Hollingworth, archbishop 1989–2001, was accused of mishandling the complaint. A report commissioned by his successor was tabled in the Queensland parliament in May 2003; it found he had let a known abuser continue as a priest in 1993. Hollingworth resigned as Governor-General on 26 May 2003, and at the Royal Commission in 2016 apologised for not pursuing claims more rigorously.
cases.cite: Diocese of Brisbane report tabled in Queensland Parliament, May 2003; ABC, BBC, The Age, May 2003 (via Wikipedia 'Peter Hollingworth')

cases.n: Salvation Army boys' homes — Australia
cases.place: Bexley and Goulburn (NSW); Indooroopilly and Riverview (Queensland); Victoria
cases.victims_note: 474 abuse cases settled in Victoria (A$15.5 million, reported 2013); about 30,000 children passed through its homes 1940s–1980s
cases.who: The Salvation Army (Australia)
cases.cover: The Royal Commission heard that officers accused of abuse were moved interstate.
cases.d: The Salvation Army sheltered about 30,000 Australian children from the 1940s to the 1980s and apologised in 2006 for abuse that may have occurred. Private settlements totalling A$15.5 million for 474 cases in Victoria were reported in 2013. In January–February 2014 the Royal Commission's Case Study 5 examined abuse at Bexley Boys' Home, Gill Memorial Home (Goulburn), Alkira (Indooroopilly) and Riverview Training Farm, and how accused officers were investigated and transferred.
cases.cite: Royal Commission Case Studies 5, 10 and 33 (2014–2015); Wikipedia 'The Salvation Army' (index)

cases.n: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
cases.place: Vancouver (Diocese of New Westminster) and Alberta (Diocese of Calgary)
cases.victims_note: 'over 300' children, mostly boys aged 3–20, over 62 years of ministry
cases.who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
cases.cover: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.
cases.d: Gordon Nakayama, a priest serving Japanese Canadian communities, abused over 300 children during 62 years of ministry. Bishop Barry Curtis charged him with immorality in 1994 after a written confession, but police were not told. In 2015 the two dioceses jointly apologised for not reporting, and in 2021 the Anglican Church of Canada and the National Association of Japanese Canadians set up a $610,000 healing fund.
cases.cite: Anglican Journal, 17 June 2015; Bulletin/Geppo, April 2021 (via Wikipedia 'Anglican Communion sexual abuse cases')

cases.n: Terry Knight — Diocese of Portsmouth
cases.who: Church of England, Diocese of Portsmouth
cases.cover: Bishop Timothy Bavin did not report Knight to police when parents raised concerns in 1985.
cases.d: Terry Knight, active in the Diocese of Portsmouth, was convicted of child sexual offences in 1996 and again in 2016. Parents had raised concerns with the bishop in 1985, who did not inform police.
cases.cite: The News (Portsmouth), 2015–2016 (via Wikipedia 'Anglican Communion sexual abuse cases')

cases.n: Dilworth School — Anglican boarding school, Auckland
cases.victims_note: police estimated 233 student victims; inquiry recorded 175 reports of sexual abuse
cases.who: Dilworth Trust (Anglican-linked school for boys from disadvantaged families)
cases.cover: The independent inquiry concluded that ongoing silence about the abuse was 'the primary reason for the damage' to former students.
cases.d: Police Operation Beverly arrested six men on 14 September 2020 over historic offences at Dilworth from the 1970s to the early 2000s; by June 2021 eleven men had been charged, including a former chaplain who pleaded guilty to abusing 16 boys. Twelve former staff were prosecuted. An independent inquiry by Silvia Cartwright and Frances Joychild, released 18 September 2023, covered 1950–2005 and recorded 175 reports of sexual abuse and 134 of serious physical abuse. The Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care also examined Dilworth.
cases.cite: Cartwright & Joychild, Dilworth independent inquiry report, 18 September 2023; RNZ, Stuff, NZ Herald 2020–2023 (via Wikipedia 'Dilworth School')

cases.n: Gloriavale Christian Community — convictions and Employment Court findings
cases.victims_note: Police said in 2021 at least 60 people in the community had been involved in 'harmful sexual behaviour'
cases.who: Gloriavale Christian Community
cases.cover: In January 2025 Gloriavale's leadership said past leaders had not reported known abuse to authorities; in 2026 the Charities Registration Board cited the school's failure to report child sexual offending.
cases.d: Founder Neville 'Hopeful Christian' Cooper was convicted in 1995 of sexual abuse of young members and jailed for five years. Police and Oranga Tamariki launched Operation Minneapolis in 2020; a former member was sentenced in March 2024 to 11 years 10 months for 26 child sexual offences, and leader Howard Temple pleaded guilty in 2025 to 12 charges involving girls. In May 2022 the Employment Court ruled in Courage v Gloriavale that three former members had been employees from age six, doing dangerous work.
cases.cite: Employment Court, Courage v Attorney-General/Gloriavale (May 2022, July 2023); RNZ, Stuff (via Wikipedia 'Gloriavale Christian Community')

cases.n: Jesus Fellowship (Jesus Army) — Operation Lifeboat and redress scheme
cases.victims_note: 601 redress applicants; the trust found about one in six children in the community were sexually abused
cases.who: Jesus Fellowship Church / Jesus Fellowship Community Trust
cases.d: After founder Noel Stanton died in 2009, Northamptonshire Police ran Operation Lifeboat into historic abuse; about ten to twelve former members were convicted of sex offences. The church's redress scheme, whose final report was published on 11 September 2024, received 601 applications, paid £7.7 million, identified 539 alleged perpetrators and accepted responsibility for 264 of them, 61% of whom were former leaders.
cases.cite: Jesus Fellowship Redress Scheme Final Report, 11 September 2024; BBC News 2019–2024 (via Wikipedia 'Jesus Army')

cases.n: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches — Star-Telegram investigation
cases.place: IFB churches in the US and Canada
cases.victims_note: 412 abuse allegations in 187 churches and institutions
cases.who: Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions
cases.d: A 2018 Fort Worth Star-Telegram investigation identified 412 allegations of sexual misconduct in 187 Independent Fundamental Baptist churches and institutions across the US and Canada, some dating back to the 1970s, and described leaders moving accused men between churches.
cases.cite: Fort Worth Star-Telegram, December 2018 (via Wikipedia 'Independent Fundamental Baptist')

cases.n: Jack Schaap — First Baptist Church of Hammond, Indiana
cases.who: First Baptist Church of Hammond / Hyles-Anderson College (IFB)
cases.d: Jack Schaap, pastor of one of the largest IFB churches, was charged in September 2012 with taking a 16-year-old girl across state lines for sex (Mann Act), pleaded guilty, and was sentenced in March 2013 to 12 years in federal prison. Earlier, deacon A.V. Ballenger was jailed in 1993 for molesting a 7-year-old in Sunday school.
cases.cite: Chicago Tribune, September 2012 and May 2022 (via Wikipedia 'First Baptist Church of Hammond')

cases.n: Samuel Bateman — FLDS splinter group, Short Creek
cases.victims_note: at least 10 minor 'wives', youngest 9
cases.who: Splinter group of the FLDS led by Samuel Bateman
cases.d: Samuel Bateman, who claimed to succeed Warren Jeffs, took more than 20 'spiritual wives' between 2019 and 2022, at least 10 of them minors. Arizona officers stopped him in Flagstaff in August 2022 with three girls aged 11 to 14 in a trailer. He pleaded guilty on 1 April 2024 to conspiracy to transport a minor for criminal sexual activity and conspiracy to kidnap, and on 9 December 2024 was sentenced to 50 years; eleven followers were also convicted.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office, District of Arizona, December 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Samuel Bateman')

cases.n: La Luz del Mundo — leader Naasón Joaquín García convicted
cases.who: La Luz del Mundo church (HQ Guadalajara, Mexico)
cases.d: Naasón Joaquín García, leader of La Luz del Mundo, was arrested at Los Angeles airport on 4 June 2019 on charges brought by the California Attorney General including forcible rape of a minor and child pornography. On 3 June 2022 he pleaded guilty to three charges related to sexually abusing children and was sentenced to 16 years 8 months. Co-defendant Alondra Ocampo pleaded guilty in October 2020 to four felony counts involving minors. In 1997 former members in Mexico had accused his father, Samuel Joaquín Flores, of abuse, but the statute of limitations had expired.
cases.cite: California Department of Justice charges, 2019–2022; Los Angeles Times, AP, BBC (via Wikipedia 'Naasón Joaquín García' and 'La Luz del Mundo')

cases.n: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
cases.who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
cases.d: In November 2021 a federal grand jury in the Central District of California indicted Quiboloy and church administrators for sex trafficking, alleging girls as young as 12 were abused, and alleging followers were brought to the US and forced to solicit donations. The Philippine Department of Justice filed child abuse and human trafficking charges in March 2024, and he was taken into custody in Davao City on 8 September 2024 after police raids on the compound. He denies the charges.
cases.cite: US indictment, C.D. Cal., November 2021; Philippine DOJ, 2024 (via Wikipedia 'Apollo Quiboloy' and 'Kingdom of Jesus Christ')

cases.n: Timothy Omotoso — Jesus Dominion International (acquitted)
cases.who: Jesus Dominion International
cases.d: Nigerian televangelist Timothy Omotoso was arrested at Port Elizabeth airport on 20 April 2017 and tried on rape, trafficking and racketeering charges, with prosecutors alleging he abused young women and girls as young as 14. On 2 April 2025 the Eastern Cape High Court acquitted him and two co-accused, finding the prosecution had not proved guilt and criticising its handling of the case.
cases.cite: Eastern Cape High Court judgment, 2 April 2025; News24, BBC (via Wikipedia 'Timothy Omotoso')

cases.n: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
cases.place: Selangor and Negeri Sembilan (later raids in 8 more states)
cases.victims_note: 402 children rescued on 11 September 2024; 625 victims aged 2–28 by end of operation; 13 suspected sodomy cases among 384 screened; 415 arrests by 23 October 2024
cases.who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
cases.d: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 children's homes run by GISB and rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17; health checks found physical injuries and signs of sexual abuse. By 23 October 2024 police had made 415 arrests. Charges included sexual assault of children by madrasah teaching assistants, human trafficking, and organised-crime charges against the group's CEO; a caretaker was jailed for 10 years on 26 September 2024.
cases.cite: Royal Malaysia Police statements, September–October 2024; The Star, Bernama, Reuters (via Wikipedia 'Global Ikhwan')

cases.n: Lev Tahor — leaders convicted of kidnapping children
cases.who: Lev Tahor (ultra-Orthodox sect)
cases.d: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leader Nachman Helbrans and Mayer Rosner kidnapped a 14-year-old girl and 12-year-old boy from their mother, who had objected to her daughter's marriage to an older man at 13, and took them to Mexico. They were convicted in a US federal court on 10 November 2021 and sentenced to 12 years each on 31 March 2022. Founder Shlomo Helbrans had been convicted in New York in 1994 of kidnapping a 13-year-old boy.
cases.cite: US federal court, 2021–2022 (via Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor', citing BBC, Times of Israel, court records)

cases.n: Lev Tahor — Guatemala removal of 160 minors
cases.who: Lev Tahor
cases.d: In December 2024 Guatemalan authorities removed 160 minors from a Lev Tahor farm compound in Oratorio after abuse and trafficking complaints; in January 2025 Interpol arrested a member in Guatemala on trafficking charges. The group had earlier fled child-protection proceedings in Quebec (2013, where authorities sought care for 127 children) and Ontario.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor' (citing Reuters, Times of Israel, 2024–2025)

cases.n: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
cases.place: ISKCON rural community boarding schools, US and India
cases.who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
cases.d: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'International Society for Krishna Consciousness' (citing Rochford 2007 and others)

cases.n: Mamou Alliance Academy — missionary children's boarding school, Guinea
cases.victims_note: 80 testimonies heard by the commission
cases.who: Christian and Missionary Alliance (C&MA)
cases.cover: Alumni wrote to C&MA headquarters about abuse from the 1980s for about ten years before an inquiry was set up.
cases.d: Mamou Alliance Academy boarded the children of C&MA missionaries in West Africa. After 30 alumni asked for an investigation in 1995, an independent commission of inquiry heard 80 testimonies and reported in April 1998 that the denomination had been negligent; it identified nine offenders, and abuse included sexual molestation and rape. The US C&MA board issued an open letter asking victims' forgiveness.
cases.cite: Independent Commission of Inquiry report, April 1998; Christianity Today, 2010 (via Wikipedia 'Christian and Missionary Alliance')

cases.n: New Tribes Mission — Fanda boarding school, Senegal
cases.who: New Tribes Mission (now Ethnos360)
cases.d: A 2010 report by GRACE (Godly Response to Abuse in the Christian Environment) documented sexual, physical and emotional abuse at the Fanda school that New Tribes Mission ran in Senegal for missionaries' children in the 1980s and 1990s. In 2023 an independent review team (IHART) commissioned by the mission examined historical allegations in Colombia, Indonesia, Mexico, the Philippines, Thailand, the US, Venezuela and Brazil.
cases.cite: GRACE report, 2010; IHART summary report, 2023 (via Wikipedia 'Ethnos360')

cases.n: New Tribes Mission missionary convicted of abusing Katukina girls in Brazil
cases.who: New Tribes Mission
cases.d: Missionary Warren Scott Kennell was arrested at Orlando International Airport in 2013 and admitted molesting four children in Brazil. In July 2014 a US federal court sentenced him to 58 years for abusing Katukina indigenous girls and possessing more than 940 images of child abuse.
cases.cite: WESH-TV 2013; New York Daily News 2014 (via Wikipedia 'Ethnos360')

cases.n: Trokosi — ritual servitude of girls at shrines
cases.victims_note: Liberation ceremonies freed 400 (2000), 126 (2001), 465 (2003), 94 (2004), 120 (2005) and 52 (2010) people from specific shrines; no national count
cases.who: Traditional shrines (Ewe in Ghana and Togo; Fon in Benin)
cases.d: Under trokosi, shrines take girls, usually young virgins, as atonement for a relative's alleged wrongdoing; they serve priests without pay, and in most shrines sexual service to the priest is treated as a duty, which defenders deny. Ghana amended its Criminal Code in 1998 to make ritual or customary servitude a crime with a minimum three-year sentence, but the practice continued and no prosecutions are recorded in the source.
cases.cite: Ghana Criminal Code (Amendment) Act 1998 (Act 554); BBC 2001; Africa Recovery 2001 (via Wikipedia 'Trokosi')

cases.n: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
cases.victims_note: Karnataka government study: 40,600 devadasis (2008); Karnataka State Women's University: over 80,000 (2018); Andhra Pradesh identified 16,624
cases.who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
cases.d: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite bans going back to the Bombay Act of 1934, the Andhra Pradesh Act of 1988 and the SC/ST Atrocities Act. A Karnataka government study counted 40,600 devadasis in 2008 and a 2018 university survey found more than 80,000.
cases.cite: Karnataka government study 2008; Karnataka State Women's University 2018; New Indian Express 2020 (via Wikipedia 'Devadasi')

nets.reach_note: Smyth's abuse in Zimbabwe and South Africa was by a Church of England-linked evangelical, not through CofE structures; recorded under Anglican Communion.
nets.d: IICSA counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and found a culture of deference and secrecy. The Peter Ball case and the Makin Review of John Smyth showed senior clergy withholding evidence; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
nets.cite: IICSA Anglican Church report, 6 October 2020; Makin Review, 7 November 2024

nets.d: National Anglican churches with documented findings: Australia (1,082 complainants 1980–2015), Canada (residential schools; Nakayama), New Zealand (Dilworth School), and southern Africa (Smyth).
nets.cite: Royal Commission (Australia) 2017; TRC Canada; Dilworth inquiry 2023; Makin Review 2024

nets.d: Largest US Protestant denomination. Journalists found about 380 accused leaders and over 700 victims in 20 years (2019); the Guidepost report (2022) found the Executive Committee stonewalled survivors and kept a private list of 703 accused ministers.

nets.hq: No central body (Hammond, Indiana was a major centre)
nets.d: Network of independent churches and colleges. A 2018 Star-Telegram investigation found 412 abuse allegations in 187 IFB churches and institutions.

nets.n: Hillsong Church / Australian Christian Churches (Assemblies of God)
nets.reach_note: Hillsong has churches in about 27–30 countries, but abuse findings concern Frank Houston in Australia and New Zealand.
nets.d: Founded 1983 by Brian and Bobbie Houston. The Royal Commission found Brian Houston did not report his father Frank Houston's abuse of a boy to police in 1999; Brian Houston was acquitted of concealment in 2023.
Formed 1977; about 2,500 allegations of child sexual abuse reported to the Royal Commission in 2017. Knox Grammar School case.

nets.reach_note: Only Australian findings were verified in this pass.
nets.d: Ran children's homes in Australia that sheltered about 30,000 children from the 1940s to 1980s; Royal Commission case studies 5, 10, 33 and 49.
nets.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse

nets.n: Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD) and Diakonie
nets.d: Federation of 20 regional Protestant churches. The 2024 ForuM study found 2,225 victims and 1,259 accused in files since 1946, with an estimate of up to 9,355 minors.

nets.n: Jehovah's Witnesses (Watch Tower Bible and Tract Society)
nets.reach_note: Norway removed state registration in December 2022 over shunning of children and others (not sexual abuse); in Japan a 2023 survey of 255 former members and children reported widespread whipping of children; Ireland: two elders were removed in 2016 after reporting a child molester to police against branch advice.
nets.d: The 'two-witness rule' and internal judicial committees kept abuse reports inside congregations. Australia's Royal Commission found 1,006 alleged perpetrators since 1950, none reported to police. Findings and judgments followed in the UK, US, Netherlands and New Zealand.
nets.cite: Royal Commission Case Study 29 report, November 2016

nets.n: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
nets.reach_note: Individual cases outside the US (e.g. an Australian leader jailed in 2017) were not verified in this pass.
nets.d: Runs an abuse help line (since 1995) staffed by social workers that routes legally risky calls to church lawyers; an AP investigation in 2022 found it helped keep abuse secret in the Bisbee, Arizona case. The church disputes this.

nets.n: Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)
nets.hq: Colorado City, Arizona / Hildale, Utah (Short Creek)
nets.reach_note: The FLDS page says members live in the western US, Mexico and Canada; no Mexican case verified.
nets.d: Polygamous sect led by Warren Jeffs (convicted 2011 of sexually assaulting girls aged 12 and 15). Girls were moved from Bountiful, British Columbia, to the US for 'marriages'. In 2015 the US Department of Labor fined members $1.96 million over child labour in the 2012 pecan harvest.
nets.cite: AP 2011; BC Supreme Court 2017, 2019; US DOL 2015

nets.reach_note: Times of Israel and Channel 4 reported a UK Haredi leader used mesirah to shield suspects; not verified further.
nets.d: The principle of mesirah (not informing on a fellow Jew to secular authorities) has been documented as discouraging reports of abuse in Melbourne, Brooklyn and Israel. Cases include Malka Leifer (Australia/Israel) and Nechemya Weberman (Brooklyn).
nets.cite: Royal Commission final report 2017, rec. 16.30; Wikipedia 'Mesirah'

nets.n: Yeshivah Centre Melbourne and Yeshiva Centre Bondi (Chabad)
nets.d: Chabad institutions examined in Royal Commission Case Study 22 (2015–2016) over responses to abuse by staff and volunteers.

nets.reach_note: Also detained in Iraq (2021) and passed through Turkey and Romania; deported from Bosnia and Herzegovina in 2022 over child abuse concerns; 17 minors rescued in Yarumal, Colombia, November 2025.
nets.d: Ultra-Orthodox sect of about 200–300 people founded in Israel in 1988 by Shlomo Helbrans, accused of child abuse and forced marriage of teenage girls. Leaders were convicted in the US in 2021 of kidnapping two children.
nets.cite: Wikipedia 'Lev Tahor' (citing BBC, Reuters, court records)

nets.d: German sect founded in Chile in 1961 by Paul Schäfer, who was convicted in 2006 of abusing 25 children. It served as a DINA torture centre under Pinochet. Germany admitted in 2016–2017 that its diplomats looked away.
nets.cite: Rettig Report 1991; Houston Chronicle/AP 2006; German Foreign Office 2016

nets.reach_note: Police investigated the group in these countries in the 1990s, without convictions; colonies in an estimated 70 countries by the mid-1970s.
nets.d: Founded by David Berg. A UK High Court judge found in 1995 that the group, including top leaders, had sexually abused minors in the past, and ordered it to denounce Berg's writings.

nets.reach_note: Australia: police searched a NSW farm in 2020, no charges announced; France listed the group in a 1995 parliamentary report on cults.
nets.d: Communal Christian group that canes children. German authorities removed 40 children in 2013 (upheld by the ECHR in 2018); New York found child labour violations at a Twelve Tribes farm in 2018.
nets.cite: ECHR, Wetjen v. Germany, 2018; Times Union, 4 June 2018

nets.reach_note: Victims included people from Mexico; not verified as a separate finding here.
nets.d: Self-help group run by Keith Raniere, convicted in 2019 of racketeering and sex trafficking; the racketeering acts included sexual exploitation of a 15-year-old.
Leader convicted in 2009 on 10 counts of transporting minors across state lines for sex; 175 years.

nets.reach_note: Present in about 58 countries; findings only in the US (and a time-barred 1997 complaint in Mexico).
nets.d: Church whose leader Naasón Joaquín García pleaded guilty in 2022 to sexually abusing children in California.

Church of Apollo Quiboloy, indicted in the US in 2021 for sex trafficking including of minors, and charged in the Philippines in 2024. FBI raided its offices in California, Texas and Hawaii in January 2020.

nets.n: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB)
nets.d: Company linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement that ran children's homes; 2024 police raids rescued 402 children and led to 415 arrests.

Network of ashrams and gurukuls; founder Asaram convicted in 2018 of raping a 16-year-old and in 2023 in a Surat sisters' case. Two boys died at the Motera gurukul in 2008; an inquiry blamed ashram negligence.
Acknowledged abuse in its boarding schools in the 1970s–80s; $15 million settlement in 2008.

nets.reach_note: Fields examined by the 2023 IHART historical abuse review; findings per country not verified.
nets.d: Evangelical mission to indigenous peoples. Abuse documented at its Fanda school in Senegal (GRACE 2010) and by a missionary convicted for abusing Katukina girls in Brazil (2014).
Closed Christian community; founder convicted 1995 of sexual abuse of young members; multiple later convictions and Employment Court rulings on child labour and servitude.
Charismatic communal church; its redress scheme identified 539 alleged perpetrators and paid £7.7 million.
nets.cite: Jesus Fellowship Redress Scheme Final Report, 2024

nets.hq: No central body (Manitoba Colony, Santa Cruz)
nets.reach_note: Colonies migrated Canada→Mexico (about 6,000, 1922–25), Canada→Paraguay (about 1,800, 1927), Mexico→Belize (about 1,700 after 1958), Paraguay→Bolivia (1954–57), Mexico/Belize→Bolivia (from 1967), Canada→Bolivia (1968). No abuse finding outside Bolivia verified here.
nets.d: Closed German-speaking farming colonies. Bolivia had about 150,000 Mennonites by 2023 (estimate). The Manitoba Colony mass-rape case led to convictions in 2011.

flows.n: Bountiful, B.C. → Utah–Arizona line (girl, 13, 'married' to Warren Jeffs)
flows.d: In 2004 Brandon and Gail Blackmore took their 13-year-old daughter from Bountiful to the Utah–Arizona line to be married to Warren Jeffs, then 48. Both were convicted in 2017 of removing a child from Canada for sexual purposes.

flows.n: Bountiful, B.C. → United States (girl, 15, taken by James Oler)
flows.d: Trial records showed Warren Jeffs directed James Oler on 23 June 2004 to bring a 15-year-old girl to the US to marry an older FLDS member. Oler was convicted in 2019 of removing a child from Canada.
flows.cite: CBC News, 29 August 2019; Salt Lake Tribune, 7 February 2017

flows.n: Melbourne → Israel (Malka Leifer flown out by her school)
flows.d: In March 2008 the school paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for headmistress Malka Leifer and four of her children after abuse allegations, without telling police. She stayed in Israel until extradited back to Australia on 25 January 2021.

After the 1982 Ruston Report on his beatings was kept from police, Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. The Makin Review called him 'a problem solved and exported to Africa'.
flows.cite: Makin Review, 7 November 2024; Church Times, 15 November 2024

flows.to: Durban, then Cape Town, South Africa
flows.d: Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, Smyth moved to South Africa in 2001, attending churches in Durban (from 2002) and Cape Town (Church on Main, 2004–2016). The Makin Review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in 2018.

flows.n: Siegburg, Germany → Chile (Paul Schäfer flees abuse warrant)
flows.d: After Siegburg authorities issued a warrant in 1959 for abusing two boys, Schäfer fled and in January 1961 settled in Chile with a small group of followers, founding Colonia Dignidad.
Charged with child abuse in Chile, Schäfer disappeared on 20 May 1997 and hid in Argentina until found in a gated community in Tortuguitas in March 2005 and returned to Chile.

flows.n: Chile → Germany (Colonia Dignidad doctor Hartmut Hopp flees)
flows.d: Colony doctor Hartmut Hopp, under house arrest awaiting trial, fled Chile for Germany in May 2011. German prosecutors sought in 2016 to enforce a five-year sentence imposed in Chile, then dropped their own investigation in May 2019.
flows.cite: Santiago Times 25 May 2011; BBC 8 June 2016 and 8 May 2019 (via Wikipedia 'Colonia Dignidad')

flows.n: New York → Mexico (Lev Tahor kidnapping of two children)
flows.d: In December 2018 Lev Tahor leaders took a 14-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy from their mother to the group in Mexico; both leaders were convicted of kidnapping in 2021. Endpoints are state/country centroids.

flows.n: Chatham-Kent, Ontario → Guatemala (Lev Tahor flees child-protection orders)
flows.d: After a Quebec court ordered 14 children into foster care in November 2013 and the group moved to Ontario, members with children left for Guatemala in 2014; nine who tried to flee via Trinidad and Tobago were returned to Canada.

Frank Houston led the Assemblies of God in New Zealand from 1965 to 1977, abusing boys there, then moved to Sydney; Assemblies of God investigations found six further credible allegations in Australia and New Zealand. Origin is a country centroid.
flows.cite: Wikipedia 'Frank Houston' and 'Hillsong Church' (citing Royal Commission Case Study 18)

flows.n: Philippines → United States (KOJC followers brought to fundraise)
flows.d: US prosecutors allege KOJC brought followers to the US on fraudulent visas and sham marriages (82 over 20 years) and forced them to solicit donations; the 2021 indictment also alleges sexual abuse of girls as young as 12. Allegations, not yet tried.

New Tribes Mission missionary Warren Scott Kennell abused Katukina girls while posted in Brazil; he was arrested on return at Orlando airport and jailed for 58 years in 2014. Brazil endpoint is a country centroid.

notes:
Scope: non-Catholic religious institutions and movements. Built under a web-search cap (the shared 200-search limit ran out partway) plus several blocked sites (BBC, Guardian, AP, IICSA, part of the Royal Commission site), so later records rely more on Wikipedia pages used as an index. Each of those records names the underlying source the page cites. Please spot-check them against primary sources before publishing.

NOT INCLUDED, with reasons and leads:
- Kenya, Shakahola / Good News International Ministries (2023): 457 deaths by Aug 2025, mostly children. Paul Mackenzie and 30 others were charged in Jan 2024 with murdering 191 children. Left out because the schema has no 'kind' for killing or starvation. Add it if the map gets a child-deaths category (source: Wikipedia 'Shakahola Forest incident').
- Nigeria, almajiri / Islamic 'rehabilitation' school raids (Kaduna Rigasa, Sept 2019; Katsina; Daura): could not open any source (BBC, Guardian and Al Jazeera blocked; no Wikipedia page). Not recorded.
- Norway, Jehovah's Witnesses: the state refused grants (Jan 2022) and removed registration (Dec 2022) because members shun people, including baptised children, which it called 'negative social control' and psychological violence. This is not sexual abuse. Litigation is ongoing; Wikipedia indexes a later Court of Appeal ruling against the state that I did not verify. Source: RNS, 16 Jan 2024.
- Japan: a 2023 survey of 255 former Jehovah's Witnesses and their children (submitted to the health ministry on 14 Mar 2023) found about 75% were whipped before starting school. It records physical abuse only, not sexual. The ministry's Dec 2022 guidance (religious coercion can count as child abuse) and the Unification Church dissolution are not verified here.
- Gurmeet Ram Rahim Singh: the source gives no minors in his convictions. Left out as the brief asked. Sogyal Rinpoche and Shambhala: no findings involving minors found. Bill Gothard / IBLP: no official finding involving minors (2014 internal review, 2016 suit dropped, 2025 Texas Supreme Court procedural ruling). Branch Davidians: the DOJ 1993 child abuse report exists but I could not open it. Scientology / Sea Org: no official finding involving minors verified. Rajneesh: none.
- Thai monk Wirapol Sukphol (extradited from the US in 2017 over sex with a minor) and Luang Pu Nen Kham: no page could be opened. Not recorded. Sri Lanka monks: not researched.
- Pakistan: AP 2017/2020 recorded as 'reported'. No count of police cases. Afghanistan madrassas: not researched. UK madrassas: IICSA's 'Child protection in religious organisations and settings' (2 Sept 2021, 38 groups) exists, but its pages were blocked, so no case was made from it. Worth adding.
- Other leads not completed: Australian Royal Commission case studies 3 (Grafton, North Coast Children's Home), 20 (Hutchins School), 36 (Church of England Boys' Society) and 42 (Anglican Diocese of Newcastle). Their findings pages showed no findings text. Also Church of Scotland; Dutch Protestant; Swedish, Finnish and Norwegian Lutheran (incl. Laestadian cases in Finland); Swiss Reformed; Amish (Ohio/Pennsylvania); Orthodox churches; UK Methodist Past Cases Review 2015; Bob Jones University GRACE report (Dec 2014: discouraged reporting); the 2022 US Justice Department investigation of the SBC; LDS cases outside the US; Colorado City/Hildale 2016 federal civil-rights verdict (town marshals acted for the FLDS); Samuel Bateman flows across state lines (states not named in the source).
- Smyth: the Makin Review gives at least 85 victims in Zimbabwe and South Africa combined. The Zambesi camp location and Smyth's Zimbabwe base are not given, so the flow uses Harare as the Zimbabwe point.
- Peter Ball: victims were teenagers and young men (17 aged about 16 and up per IICSA; 18 'young men' at sentencing). Whether all were minors is not stated, so the record says 'teenagers and young men'.
- Family International: the Argentina and Australia raids ended without convictions, so the status is 'alleged'. The 1995 UK judgment is the official finding of past abuse.
- Coordinates: places given at city level. 'llc': true marks country centroids.
- Mennonite migrations (Canada→Mexico→Belize/Paraguay→Bolivia) are recorded in the old-colony-mennonites net's reach_note, not as flows, because they are community migrations and not movements of victims or offenders.
